idiom_name: pull interfaces: database/sql Rows cursor, io.Reader and bufio.Scanner, streamed http.Response.Body
implementation_notes: Go expresses the stages with small interfaces instead of a resource abstraction: db.Query returns an *sql.Rows cursor whose rows are fetched by Next/Scan and whose Close must be deferred (the documentation notes it releases the resources however the function returns, and that looping all the way through closes it implicitly), http.Response delivers the headers with the body still unread behind an io.Reader, and bufio.Scanner streams delimited records. A shared expensive stage is acquired once with sync.Once/OnceValue or a pool and handed out as an interface value, so holders depend on the pull interface rather than on a concrete provider. The classic structure is still justified when the later stages must be gated, resumed or audited, because Go supplies the primitives but leaves the stage plan, the retry of a failed middle stage and the release of the stages actually acquired to the caller.
pitfalls: Forgetting rows.Close() (directly or via defer) holds a connection from the pool until it is reclaimed, so the expensive stage stays occupied by a function that has already returned.
Skipping the rows.Err() check makes a failure in the middle of the stream look like a normal end of data - the partial-acquisition form of a silent truncation.

Reading resp.Body with io.ReadAll, or not closing it at all, turns the staged transfer back into a full acquisition and prevents connection reuse, because the transport can only recycle a consumed body.
bufio.Scanner stops with an error when a token exceeds its buffer limit, so records larger than the configured maximum fail at a stage boundary instead of streaming.
json.Decoder streams a document but leaves trailing content unread, so a partially consumed decoder must not be mistaken for a validated payload.
